pages.title: Supplier Quote Template: MOQ, Freight & Total Cost
pages.description: Download a supplier quote CSV and compare three fictional quotes for 300 units. See how MOQ, pack size and freight change the cheapest option.
pages.deck: The lowest unit price can require the largest cash outlay. Compare the quantity you must actually order, then add the known freight and setup charges.
pages.body:
Worked example: buying 300 identical bottles

All three fictional suppliers quote in EUR, with equivalent specifications and freight to the same destination. This is a calculation example, not a list of suppliers you can buy from.

QuoteUnit priceMOQ / packFreight + setupOrder unitsKnown cost
Sample A€2.10500 / 100€250 + €50500€1,350
Sample B€2.45200 / 50€90 + €0300€825
Sample C€1.901,000 / 100€350 + €801,000€2,330

Sample B has the highest unit price but the lowest known outlay for this order. Sample C leaves 700 extra units. A lower per-unit cost is not automatically a better use of cash.

The calculation you can reproduce

order_units = ceil(max(required_units, MOQ) / pack_size) × pack_size
known_cost = order_units × unit_price + freight + setup
cost_per_ordered_unit = known_cost / order_units

For B: ceil(max(300, 200) / 50) × 50 = 300 units. The known cost is 300 × €2.45 + €90 = €825. Cost per ordered unit is €2.75. The RFQ Desk example uses the same data and required quantity.

How to use the CSV

  1. Download the file or select the sample in the calculator.
  2. Use one row per supplier and keep all seven headers unchanged.
  3. Enter one currency for the entire comparison and set required units to 300.
  4. Replace fictional figures only with confirmed quotes. A blank freight charge is unknown; zero means confirmed zero.
  5. Export the comparison, then ask suppliers about exclusions before ordering.

What is missing from the total?

Duty, tax, insurance, inspection, payment fees, financing and unquoted delivery charges are excluded. Align freight scope, destination, specifications and payment terms first. This is a known-cost comparison, not a complete landed-cost estimate or a supplier recommendation.

What happens after the quote?

Once a purchase order and invoice exist, use the two-way invoice-matching example to understand unit-price differences and cumulative invoiced quantities. It does not authorize a payment.

pages.title: Purchase Order vs Invoice Matching: A €44 Worked Example
pages.description: Learn two-way PO and invoice matching with a fictional €44 price difference and 20-unit overbilling example. Download the source JSON and try TradeCheck.
pages.deck: Two-way matching compares the invoice with the purchase order. It can reveal price and quantity exceptions, but it cannot prove that goods arrived or that payment is safe.
pages.body:
One invoice, two different exceptions

The fictional PO orders 300 bottles at €2.50 and 100 lids at €0.40. The current invoice bills 220 bottles at €2.70 and 100 lids at €0.40. An earlier invoice already billed 100 bottles.

CheckCalculationFinding
Current bottle price220 × (€2.70 − €2.50)€44 price variance
Cumulative bottle quantity100 prior + 220 current − 300 ordered20 units above the PO
Current invoice arithmetic220 × €2.70 + 100 × €0.40€634, matching its stated total

A mathematically correct invoice can still disagree with the purchase order. The €44 is a calculated price exception, not money that has been recovered.

Reproduce it in TradeCheck

  1. Download the source JSON or choose the fictional example in TradeCheck.
  2. Confirm PO ID, invoice PO reference, supplier, currency, line references and units.
  3. Run the review and inspect exceptions together with their source references.
  4. Export the evidence report or an unsent supplier question draft.

The local MCP exposes the same deterministic review. Read the MCP installation guide before connecting it to your assistant.

Missing history is not a clean result

Without the earlier 100-unit invoice, the current 220 units alone do not exceed 300. If the history is unknown, the report must preserve that gap. Do not turn an empty list of known prior invoices into a claim that no prior invoices exist. Source references are labels supplied by the caller; the tool has not independently read a PDF.

Two-way versus three-way matching

Three-way matching adds goods-receipt evidence. TradeCheck performs two-way checks only: it does not read receipts, authenticate suppliers, check a bank-account change or approve payments. A clean arithmetic result still needs the organization's receipt and approval process.

Starting with an Excel export?

The browser importer accepts CSV, TSV and pasted table rows with explicit column mapping. Review the preview, enter invoice totals and confirm the extraction. It does not perform OCR. See the table import guide for required fields.

pages.title: AI API Cost Tracking Template: Billed Spend by Project
pages.description: Download a normalized AI usage CSV. Calculate billed spend per 1,000 requests, monthly pace and cost per customer with a fully worked fictional example.
pages.deck: Start from billed cost when reconciling API spending. Token counts alone cannot account for every discount, cache rate, tool charge or billing adjustment.
pages.body:
A 14-day example with three cost buckets

These provider and model labels are fictional. They illustrate the normalized format accepted by ModelMeter, not current provider prices.

Project / modelRequestsBilled USDUSD / 1,000 requests
Support / Fast model12,000$48$4
Research / Reasoning model500$86$172
Support / Backup model800$6$7.50

Total billed spend is $140 over 14 complete days. Research accounts for $86 / $140 = 61.43% of that spend, despite having fewer requests. This identifies a bucket to inspect; it does not establish that the model is wasteful or replaceable.

Monthly pace is an assumption

monthly_pace = billed_spend / complete_days × days_in_month
$140 / 14 × 30 = $300
$300 / 40 active_customers = $7.50 per customer

This calculation assumes the remaining days behave like the observed days. A launch, trial cohort or traffic spike can invalidate it. It is neither a forecast nor your next invoice. An entered $300 monthly budget is exactly matched by this example's pace.

Prepare a comparable export

  1. Keep project, provider, model, requests, input_tokens, output_tokens and billed_usd headers.
  2. Aggregate to non-overlapping rows for the same complete time window.
  3. Reconcile the billed USD column with the provider's invoice or dashboard. Resolve currency conversion and credits outside this tool.
  4. Enter complete days, calendar days in the month and the customer count for your chosen definition.
  5. Review expensive groups before changing routing, quality thresholds or quotas.

What does this report omit?

Costs absent from your CSV remain absent, including infrastructure, storage, retrieval, tool calls and support. Provider-native exports are not automatically mapped. Input and output tokens are retained as context; ModelMeter does not apply a hidden price table to them. Files are processed locally, with no provider key required.

pages.title: SQL Revenue Practice: Paid Orders, Refunds & GROUP BY
pages.description: Work through a six-row orders dataset in SQLite. Filter paid orders, subtract refunds and produce a country report with expected results and downloadable SQL.
pages.deck: Build a small report from six orders. The exercise definition is simple: count paid orders and subtract their refunds; exclude cancelled orders.
pages.body:
The fictional orders table

IDCustomerCountryStatusRevenueRefund
1AdaDEpaid1200
2BoFRpaid8020
3AdaDEcancelled500
4CyDEpaid9090
5DiFRpaid2000
6BoFRpaid400

1. Select paid orders

SELECT id, customer
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
ORDER BY id;

Expected IDs: 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6. Order 4 remains a paid order even though it was fully refunded. Order 3 is cancelled and must not contribute to this exercise.

2. Calculate net revenue

SELECT SUM(revenue - refund) AS net_revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid';

Expected result: 420. The paid gross amounts total 530 and refunds total 110. Counting the cancelled order would incorrectly return 470.

3. Report by country

SELECT country, SUM(revenue - refund) AS net_revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY net_revenue DESC, country ASC;

Expected rows: FR = 300, then DE = 120. The second sort key makes equal totals deterministic. The browser checks queries against a second dataset too, so a hard-coded 420 is not a solution.

What this teaches, and what it does not

Practice WHERE before aggregation, SUM of a row-level expression, GROUP BY and a stable ORDER BY. This toy definition is not a revenue-recognition policy. Real finance reports may require tax, currencies, settlement dates, partial refunds and duplicate prevention. SQLite runs locally; there is no production database connection.

Syntax reference: SQLite SELECT documentation.

pages.title: SEC Company Facts: Match Exact Periods Before Comparing
pages.description: Understand SEC financial fact periods, filing dates and accession links. Compare one exact fact across filing cutoffs with a fictional worked example.
pages.deck: A reporting period and a filing date answer different questions. Match entity, concept, unit and exact period first; then compare what was available at each filing cutoff.
pages.body:
One annual period, two reported values

FilingLens's fictional example reports revenue for 1 January–31 December 2024 as 125,000,000 USD at an earlier filing cutoff and 123,000,000 USD at a later cutoff. The absolute difference is −2,000,000 USD. These are illustrative values from a fictional company, not a real issuer disclosure.

The comparison asks what value was available for the same period at two cutoffs. It does not compare one year's revenue with another year's revenue.

Keep these fields separate

FieldQuestion it answersCommon mistake
CIKWhich reporting entity?Treating a ticker as a numeric CIK
Concept and unitWhat is measured, in what units?Comparing USD with per-share facts
Start / end datesWhat exact period does the value cover?Mixing quarterly and year-to-date revenue
Filed dateWhen was the filing submitted?Treating the filing date as the financial period
AccessionWhich filing contains the reported context?Treating a link as proof someone read the filing

Reproduce an evidence check

  1. Start with the fictional example, or use the browser's Apple total-assets lookup for live SEC data.
  2. Select one exact period and unit from the available observations.
  3. Choose two filing-date cutoffs. The tool selects the latest eligible filed date at each cutoff.
  4. Read both values and the absolute difference, then follow the real accession links to the filings.
  5. Export the source note and record any unresolved context before drawing a conclusion.

Missing and conflicting values

No observation before a cutoff means incomplete evidence, not zero. Different values reported on the same selected filing date remain ambiguous. Two cutoffs can correctly select the same filing and produce no change. A changed value alone does not prove a restatement or explain its cause.

Data and tool boundaries

The live browser lookup uses the SEC companyconcept API for a small allowlist of US-GAAP concepts. An uploaded file is not authenticated. The local MCP performs comparisons only and does not fetch data. Neither interface provides trading signals. Read the methodology and setup guide.

Primary source: SEC EDGAR API documentation. Check original filings for the financial and reporting context.

pages.title: Shopify Translation CSV Checklist: Keys, Text & Imports
pages.description: Check a Shopify translation export before editing it. See the required columns, duplicate-key pitfalls and a fictional product example you can download.
pages.deck: Keep a backup of the Shopify translations export. Preserve the row identity, leave existing translations intact and review protected names and numbers before importing edited text.
pages.body:
A safe practice file

The download contains three fictional product rows, not products from your shop. Its first row is an untranslated German title: Cedar insulated bottle, 750 ml. A second row already contains a German translation. A third row contains HTML and falls outside this pilot's supported text fields.

RowInputChecker result
Product 1001 / title / deBlank translation, plain product titleEligible for the pilot's text workflow
Product 1002 / title / deExisting translated textKept unchanged
Product 1003 / body_html / deHTML descriptionKept unchanged; outside pilot scope

Eight columns to preserve

Type,Identification,Field,Locale,Market,Status,Default content,Translated content

The checker requires these unique headers. A general product export is a different file. The combination of Type, Identification, Field, Locale and Market identifies a translation row; duplicate keys are rejected. Keep the original identifiers instead of substituting a product title or spreadsheet row number.

Before your next import

  1. Export translations from Shopify Settings → Languages and keep an untouched backup.
  2. Check a small batch in LocaleBatch. The free checker handles 1–500 rows and a file under 700 KB.
  3. Review eligible rows. This pilot handles PRODUCT title, meta_title and meta_description text in its listed languages.
  4. Protect your brand names, model labels, placeholders and numeric claims. Keeping those strings does not prove that the translation is linguistically correct.
  5. Have a competent speaker review the text, then test a small import and inspect the storefront before scaling.

Does the free checker translate my store?

No. Your own CSV is checked locally; the delivery demonstration uses fixed example translations. Paid AI translation and store publishing are unavailable. The tool cannot prove that a Shopify import will succeed or that the translated copy is legally or commercially suitable.

Shopify's import instructions

Shopify supports translation export and import through CSV. Follow the current Shopify translation documentation when exporting, selecting import options and publishing languages. LocaleBatch is an independent checker and is not endorsed by Shopify.
